newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Ailing Singapore stock market seen ripe for rally.
newsitem.headline: Ailing Singapore stock market seen ripe for rally.

text.p: Singapore's ailing stock market, squeezed by an economic slowdown and the sparkling rise of rival bourses, is now undervalued and ripe for a rally, analysts say.
"Valuations are getting very attractive and I don't think the potential downside is very great," said Violet Soh, head of research at brokerage Fraser Securities.

Almost all parts of the Singapore economy have felt the pinch this year. Heavily dependent on electronics and computer products, its manufacturing industries have seen exports dwindle thanks to a slump in demand in U.S. and Asian markets.

After expanding 10.9 percent year-on-year in the first quarter, Singapore's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 7.0 percent in the second quarter and is expected to rise just 3.5 percent in the third, economists say.

Banking and finance companies have seen their margins eroded by new credit controls, and property developers, which enjoyed a boom from spiralling house prices in the early 1990s, have seen their bubble burst by government measures to curb speculation.
As a result, Singapore's benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index has fallen by 17 percent to 2,077 points from its high of over 2,500 points at the beginning of February.

While most chartists are unwilling to predict an immediate rebound, most analysts looking at the fundamentals of the Singapore stock market say it has now fallen too far and shows signs of being ready for a rally.
"The Singapore market has reached a level where a lot of the bad news has been discounted," said Mano Sabnani, director of research at DBS Securities. "The selling has exhausted itself."
Analysts say several reliable indicators now point to a rise in the stock market. The most obvious is relative value.

While the Singapore market has been losing ground, New York and Hong Kong have both outperformed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average has risen 17 percent this year while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index has roared ahead by 24 percent.
These spectacular gains have drawn funds away from Singapore and exaggerated short-term cyclical problems from which its economy would shortly recover, Sabnani said.

"So Singapore's DBS-50 (index of leading stocks) is now trading at a price earnings (PE) ratio of below 17 times for 1996 and only 15 times for 1997," he said. "Singapore has traditionally traded between 17 and 25 times."
He said another indicator was a widening gap between equity yields at about 5.5 percent and local bank rates at 3.0 percent.
"Whenever the earnings yield gap stretches above two percentage points, it will catch the eye of investors," he said.
An institutional broker with a large banking group said there were already discreet signs that some local stocks were beginning to pick up.
"Electronics companies are gleaning more interest," he said, noting the 54 percent net profit rise reported last week by semi-conductor testing company Sunright Ltd.
Other analysts said the most likely Singapore companies to show an early rebound were banks and industrial blue chips such as Keppel Corp.
